name: Plain Language
title: Plain Language
answer: Plain language means rewriting school policies, notices, and forms so families can actually understand them, rather than leaving them in legal or jargon-heavy wording. AI can help produce a plain version quickly, but a staff member must check it for accuracy before it goes out. This matters because families act on what they understand, and clear English also translates better for families who speak other languages.

sections.body: School documents are frequently written in a style suited to lawyers rather than parents, and policies, notices, and forms packed with jargon can leave families confused or intimidated. The problem is not that families do not care, but that the wording itself gets in the way of understanding and action. Plain, supportive language is the fix, and AI is well suited to turning complex text into a version most families can read. A district can use an approved tool to rewrite a policy explanation, a permission form, or a notice at an accessible reading level. The aim is communication that families can act on, not wording that protects the institution.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, a staff member takes an existing document such as a policy explanation, a permission form, or a notice and runs it through an approved AI tool to produce a plain language version. That staff member then checks the plain version for accuracy and confirms that nothing important was lost in the rewrite. Where a legal notice must keep certain wording, the plain explanation is added alongside the original rather than replacing it. The same care applies before translation, because a clear English original produces a clearer translation in any language. The text does not give grade band variations, so the practice applies to family-facing documents across the school rather than to a specific age group.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with evidence from two sources. The truancy trial showed that plain, supportive language gets better results than legal wording (Lasky-Fink et al., 2021). Research on machine translated school notices found that translations of complex English text often backfired with Spanish speaking families (Rodriguez-Castro, 2018). The author of that work proposed checking readability before translating. The text states no further figures or findings beyond these.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text. A staff member, not the AI tool, checks that the plain version is accurate and that nothing important was lost. Legal notices may need to keep certain wording, so plain language is added as an explanation alongside rather than substituted for the required text. Readability should be checked before translating, since complex English produces translations that can backfire. The decisions about what a document must say, what can be simplified, and what is accurate stay with people.
